webTitle: Iran accuses US of ‘war crime’ after missile blast kills four people at wedding

fields.headline: Iran accuses US of ‘war crime’ after missile blast kills four people at wedding
fields.trailText: Blast also injures 68 guests at the wedding in southern Iran, prompting fears of escalation in hostilities
fields.bodyText: Iran has accused the US of a war crime after a missile blast killed at least four people and injured 68 who were attending a wedding at a private home in a coastal city of southern Iran, as the fresh exchange of strikes prompted fears of a wider renewal of hostilities. Iranian media said that the wedding ceremony was being held in a home in the city of Kuhestak, Hormozgan province, late on Tuesday when a US missile struck, with shrapnel and debris from the strike killing and injuring people. Among the dead was a four-year-old child, Amir-Ali Karimi, and a 16-year-old, Mohammad Mollahi. “It’s a terrible thing. I’m extremely worried and upset about what happened – really upset,” Ali Mollahi, the father of the bride, told Mehr News. A video of the aftermath shows colourful wedding streamers and decorations strewn across the ground, and shoes abandoned in the rush to escape the attack. “You wicked people have attacked people’s homes and turned their wedding ceremony into a funeral,” said a man filming the aftermath of the strike, shared by Fars news agency. The deputy of the provincial government, Ahmad Nafisi, said first responders had headed immediately to the scene and transferred the wounded to the hospitals. Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson called the US attack a “war crime” and said Iran “will respond to these savage crimes with firmness”. The chief Iranian negotiator, Mohammad Baqer Ghalibaf, said the attack had killed families with children, and called the US the “great Satan”. “If a power acts like Satan, picks targets like Satan and kills like Satan, it’s Satan. Shields a junior Satan that does the same? It’s THE Great Satan,” Ghalibaf said in a post on X. The US attacks followed strikes on Sunday, ending a month-long uneasy truce between the US and Iran, and appeared to signal a resumption of another cycle of escalation. US Central Command (Centcom) said the overnight strikes focused on Iranian military targets, including air defence sites, radars and maritime assets. Iran responded by launching drones and missiles on US bases across the Middle East, including in Bahrain, Kuwait and the UAE. Iran’s military spokesperson, Lt Col Ebrahim Zolfaghari, vowed “heavier, broader, and more crushing and devastating” retaliation. Videos of the aftermath of the strike show a caved-in roof, blown-out windows and ground riddled with debris, as well as walls pockmarked with what appeared to be holes from shrapnel. Footage from a nearby hospital showed women in wedding attire watching as injured children were being treated. “When we arrived there, an explosion occurred. It was very intense. Bricks, stones and cement hit me in the face and head, and many others were injured,” a child who was injured at the wedding told the state-affiliated Fars news agency. A woman with her hands decorated in henna for the nuptials posted a video on Instagram after the attack, saying “my hands and feet are still shaking”. A spokesperson for Centcom, Tim Hawkins, said the US was aware of reports of civilian casualties, but the “US military never targets civilians, unlike the [Iranian Revolutionary Guards Corps]”. In February, a strike on an elementary school killed at least 156 people, including more than 120 schoolchildren. Independent investigations concluded that the US likely carried out the strike with the assistance of AI, though the US government said the incident remained under investigation. Pictures of shrapnel collected at the site of Tuesday’s attack were published on Iranian state media, and appeared to show the internal components of US munitions. Trevor Ball, an independent weapons analyst, identified some of the remnants as belonging to the Standoff Land Attack Missile-Expanded Response (Slam-Er) missile, which is made by the US weapons company Boeing. The Slam-Er is a 1,500-pound, GPS-guided missile touted by Boeing to be “extremely accurate”. It was unclear if the home where the wedding was being held was struck directly, or if a missile hit close to the home and debris from the strike hit the home and its occupants. CCTV footage captured at least six strikes in the area within a minute. A separate strike appeared to hit a communications tower about 150 metres away from the home. Authorities said that several “telecommunications and internet towers and sites were also seriously damaged in the latest strikes”. The US has been targeting communications and radar infrastructure along Iran’s coast to try to stop its blockade on the strait of Hormuz, a chokepoint which prior to the US-Iran war was a transit point for at least 20% of the world’s oil supply. Iran has virtually closed the strait since the start of the Iran war, frustrating the US president, Donald Trump, who is facing a midterm election with expensive gas prices and knock-on inflation across the board. In recent weeks, the US has focused on trying to degrade Iran’s capacity to strike ships transiting the strait to reopen the waterway for traffic.

webTitle: ‘He’s a good man’: George Clooney defends Mark Ruffalo in Paramount-Warner Bros merger row

fields.headline: ‘He’s a good man’: George Clooney defends Mark Ruffalo in Paramount-Warner Bros merger row
fields.trailText: ‘I worry whenever big companies are consolidating,’ Clooney said at Venice film festival, supporting Ruffalo’s right to criticise the deal amid antisemitism accusations
fields.bodyText: George Clooney has defended Mark Ruffalo’s right to criticise the proposed $111bn Paramount takeover of Warner Bros Discovery, saying he is concerned about the consequences of further consolidation in Hollywood. Speaking in Venice ahead of receiving the festival’s Golden Lion for lifetime achievement, Clooney said he supported Ruffalo’s “ability to speak freely” about the proposed merger, while expressing his own doubts about the deal. “I worry when a big company swallows up another company,” Clooney said. “I always worry whenever big companies are consolidating because it means a lot of people are going to lose their jobs.” Ruffalo has emerged as one of the most outspoken opponents of the Paramount-Warner Bros deal. In a social media post last month, the Marvel star attacked the proposed merger over its potential consequences for Hollywood, while also turning his criticism on the family behind Paramount. David Ellison, the company’s chief executive, is the son of Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison, and Ruffalo accused the Ellison family of being complicit the “genocide” of Palestinians, arguing that it was “built on an apartheid system of oppression powered by Oracle”. Ruffalo highlighted Oracle’s ties to the Israeli military, sharing a video of the company’s executive vice-chair and Paramount board member Safra Catz discussing technologies Oracle had used after the 7 October Hamas attack on Israel. His comments prompted a backlash from Paramount, which accused him of invoking antisemitic tropes. Ruffalo rejected the accusation and has continued to defend his criticism of the deal and of Oracle’s business ties to Israel. More than 170 Jewish artists, academics and public figures subsequently signed an open letter defending the actor and warning against attempts to silence criticism of Israel or the proposed merger. “I support Mark Ruffalo’s ability to speak freely,” Clooney said. “I think that that’s ridiculous. We’re not going to ban speech. I believe in free speech even when I completely disagree with it. That’s important, right? In fact, it’s part of how a democracy works. “There are going to be people tonight in the room that are going to disagree with most everything I say or stand for. Fair enough. That’s how it’s supposed to be. We’re supposed to argue these things out and come to a conclusion based on the information that we take in … I will always support Mark Ruffalo’s ability to speak freely. I like him. He’s a good man.” Clooney said he did not believe the Paramount-Warner deal necessarily made financial sense. “I don’t know how this goes through. There are so many issues involved,” he said. Clooney also warned that artificial intelligence will become “a very big part of this industry” but will “hurt us in a lot of ways”. He joked: “I would like to avoid being in a tampon commercial 20 years after I’m dead.” The prominent Trump critic said the US midterm elections in November “should be a check and balance”, adding that in 2028 “with any luck, we’ll have some restoration into normalcy”. He also raised concerns about the concentration of media ownership among the world’s wealthiest people. Asked about the state of journalism, he pointed to Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, owner of the Washington Post, and Elon Musk, owner of X. Clooney will accept the lifetime achievement award on Wednesday evening. It is a striking case of life imitating art: last year, he attended the festival for Noah Baumbach’s Jay Kelly, in which he played an ageing Hollywood star travelling to Italy to receive a lifetime achievement honour. Clooney will now undergo the same ritual in real life, with Laura Dern – his Jay Kelly co-star – presenting the award. The honour caps a relationship with Venice stretching back almost three decades. Clooney first appeared at the festival with Out of Sight in 1998 and has returned with films including Good Night, and Good Luck, Michael Clayton and Gravity.

webTitle: US-Iran hostilities resume amid concerns at Hegseth’s military leadership | First Thing

fields.headline: First Thing: US-Iran hostilities resume amid concerns at Hegseth’s military leadership
fields.trailText: Leading Democrat accuses secretary of defense of causing ‘lasting harm’ to US forces
fields.bodyText: Good morning. The US has launched more airstrikes on Iranian targets, prompting counterstrikes by Tehran targeting American interests in Bahrain, Kuwait, Jordan and Iraq. The six-month conflict had shifted into an economic standoff before this weekend’s strikes, but recent promises by both sides to respond to further attacks have highlighted how quickly the conflict could spill back into military action. The Iranian Red Crescent said four people, including a child, were killed and more than 50 were injured when shrapnel from a US missile attack hit a home where a wedding celebration was taking place in the city of Kuhestak. The US central command spokesperson Capt Tim Hawkins said: “The US military never targets civilians.” Why are there concerns about US military leadership? A senior Democrat accused Pete Hegseth of having “hollowed out” the army’s senior ranks after its top civilian leader, Daniel Driscoll, resigned. Senator Jack Reed said: “It is far past time for Trump to recognize the lasting harm Pete Hegseth is inflicting on the Department of Defense … cultivating a culture where dissent is punished and competence is secondary to personal allegiance.” How do officials appear to have profited from AI stocks? Emil Michael, a Pentagon official who is overseeing military artificial intelligence policy, reaped profits this year of up to $24m by selling his private investment in Elon Musk’s AI company. He has now sold his holdings in another AI company for between $5m and $25m, according to records seen by the Guardian. Trump homeland security chief says ICE agents could be sent to polling places In another move that threatens to intimidate voters at November’s midterms, the US homeland security secretary, Markwayne Mullin, on Tuesday said that federal immigration and customs enforcement (ICE) officers could be deployed to polling sites across the country. Mullin said: “ICE’s job is immigration, customs enforcement. If we’re serving a warrant we will be where we need to be.” In a separate statement, the department said: “ICE conducts intelligence-driven targeted enforcement, and if an active public safety threat endangered a polling location, they may be arrested as a result of that targeted enforcement action.” Federal law prohibits military personnel or other “armed” agents from being “at any place where a general or special election is held”. What has a whistleblower identified as a risk to mail-in ballots? A new system to screen millions of mail-in ballots for the midterms was thrown together so hastily, and tested so little, that a single scanning glitch could mean entire batches of ballots are turned away, a whistleblower has told Congress. Tucson police investigate deadly shooting outside gay bar as hate crime Authorities in Tucson, Arizona, are investigating a shooting outside a gay bar that left three people dead as a possible hate crime. Police said: “Initial evidence suggests the suspect confronted the victims in the parking lot. The suspect was in possession of a note with several LGBTQIA+ associated businesses written on it. The department is currently investigating this homicide as a hate crime.” What is the latest legal setback to the Trump administration’s attack on LGBT+ rights? A federal judge has dismissed the Trump administration’s lawsuit challenging California’s policy of allowing transgender youth to play on sports teams. The justice department had been fighting for a year to force California to ban trans girls from women’s sports, with the president directly singling out one trans track and field athlete in online attacks. US officials defend Venezuela oil deal amid questions over rebuilding plan Trump administration officials have defended a highly contentious deal giving the US control of a significant chunk of Venezuelan oil reserves. Last week, Donald Trump announced a deal that would give the US “majority” control over 65bn barrels – roughly one-fifth – of Venezuela’s oil reserves. US officials said the agreement would create a stable economic platform to restore Venezuelan democracy after nearly three decades of autocratic rule, but the pact has provoked outrage among Venezuela’s opposition, already furious that democracy has yet to return to the country eight months after the removal of Nicolás Maduro by US special forces. In other news … The accused in the killing of Charlie Kirk, Tyler Robinson, must stand trial and is eligible for the death penalty, a judge has ruled. The Democratic contender Abdul El-Sayed has hit back at JD Vance after the vice-president described him as representative of “terrible evil”. The incumbent senator Ed Markey, 80, has won the Massachusetts Democratic primary despite his opponent claiming he was too old to be effective. Tiger Woods is set to change his not guilty plea in the DUI case stemming from a crash in Florida this year. A federal judge dismissed the remaining claims against Lizzo’s production company, declaring the case brought by her former wardrobe stylist could not proceed. Stat of the day: USS Abraham Lincoln arrives at Thai port after gruelling 270 days at sea The US aircraft carrier at the center of a row over conditions on board after months at sea as part of Trump’s war against Iran has finally arrived at a Thai port. Reports of deteriorating living conditions and poor mental health on the vessel have made headlines around the world. Well Actually: How do you define good health – and achieve it – in a broken US medical system? Elle Hunt speaks to Dr Lucy McBride, whose new book aims to help people navigate US healthcare – and to tread carefully in the wellness industry. Don’t miss this: As Nepal’s morgues fill, Parkrit hopes her DNA can be used to find her mother Cait Kelly has been in Kathmandu in the aftermath of the devastating floods in Nepal. A week on from the disaster, she reports how authorities are urging relatives of the thousands of missing and dead to provide blood samples. … or this: Modern Family’s Mitch and Cam on their hilarious and groundbreaking love The on-screen love between Mitchell (Jesse Tyler Ferguson) and Cameron (Eric Stonestreet) in Modern Family was a rare example of a gay couple raising a child on TV. Hannah Verdier has spoken to the two actors whose chemistry made them one of the most adored on-screen couples of the era. Climate check: Global heating will hit at least 1.8C, UN warns, and there are ‘no good outcomes’ A report by the UN Environment Programme has confirmed overshooting the 1.5C goal inscribed in the Paris agreement is now “unavoidable”. It said the best hope to limit the impact was to adopt an “overshoot, peak and decline” pathway, but that human health, water supplies, nature, cities, infrastructure and economies could all be severely damaged, and some losses would be irreversible. Last Thing: Australian police investigate after 5,500 sheep stolen from farm It sounds like a heist at an incredible scale. Queensland police are investigating after about 5,500 Dorper sheep worth more than $1.2m USD were allegedly stolen from a farm in western Queensland. webTitle: Trump’s threat against an NBC journalist is an attack on reality | Margaret Sullivan

fields.headline: Trump’s threat against an NBC journalist is an attack on reality
fields.trailText: The president’s call for the FCC to scrutinize Kristen Welker’s innocuous remarks is a sign of desperation
fields.bodyText: With his approval ratings tanking, the crucial midterm elections looming, and his war with Iran turning into a quagmire, Donald Trump has entered full freak-out mode. It’s not hard to tell. Just look at what happened this week when he lashed out at Kristen Welker, the well-respected host of NBC’s Meet the Press, and one of the best-known journalists in the nation. Welker observed recently that Trump – while having significant influence – has a “mixed record” on making successful endorsements this year. An innocuous statement, made in advance of the Sunday show during her analytical comments to a network affiliate station in Washington. But not harmless in Trump’s opinion. Furious, he called on the Federal Communications Commission to go after Welker, saying she “will be reported to the FCC for rebuke or punishment”. In fact, as the Hill newspaper reported this week, while Trump “boasts a 100 percent record in Senate Republican primary contests this election cycle, several of his high-profile gubernatorial picks have lost”. That sounds like a mixed record, doesn’t it? Not to Trump, who called Welker’s comments “purposeful inaccuracy”. “The Press is a Disgrace to our Nation, and I hope that Chairman Brendan Carr, and the fine people of his Commission, will take this Threat to our Country very seriously,” he wrote on Truth Social. He later added: “FCC to the rescue.” The threat is absurd. It would seem even more so if Trump had not already been using the agency as a weapon in his long-running campaign against the reality-based press. Carr is a partisan, fully devoted to Trump’s mission, and he has shown himself more than willing to do the bidding of the president who appointed him during this second presidential term. The FCC is intended to be bipartisan and independent but under Trump, it has skewed heavily Maga – and clearly political. Carr himself seems to embrace without embarrassment the role of Trump’s media attack dog. He has warned that he would use the FCC’s power to issue broadcast licenses to go after what he and his boss call “fake news”. The skirmishes are widespread. ABC has sued the FCC, charging that the agency’s early review of eight local broadcast licenses violates the first amendment. The FCC is supposed to adhere to first amendment restrictions in dealing with broadcast licenses or in any punitive measures at all. “While the FCC has the limited ability to revoke stations’ broadcast licenses, it has not done so in over 40 years and its powers do not include revoking licenses because of a disagreement over a viewpoint expressed on the station,” the Washington Post noted this week. It’s no surprise that Trump has singled out Welker for this unwarranted attack. He has a long and shameful history of going after female journalists and seems to particularly relish criticizing female journalists of color. In his first term, his targets included Yamiche Alcindor, then of PBS, April Ryan of American Urban Radio and Abby Phillip of CNN. In one particularly vicious moment, he went after Welker herself during an interview earlier this year, saying: “You’re either crooked or you’re stupid.” This new attack on Welker brings together some of his favorite techniques – trashing a Black female journalist, cracking down on free speech in apparent violation of first amendment protections and using what should be an independent government body (including, of course, the justice department) to carry out his retaliation efforts. Although this new chapter is part of a well-established pattern, it feels especially desperate when seen in context. In recent days, Trump’s efforts to control the media through threats and punishment have ramped up. The administration has barred reporters from three major news organizations from covering the G20 meetings, even as top journalists at Stars and Stripes, the military newspaper with a long history of independence, have been fired. Trump’s reality has turned sour, so he certainly doesn’t want that reality reflected in the news media. Threatening Kristen Welker – like so much of what he’s doing – is obvious over-reach. If the FCC does somehow attempt to punish her or her network, there’s a solid first amendment case to be made in response. NBC, which has staunchly defended Welker, is likely to make it. Welker did nothing wrong, not in terms of the facts and not in terms of her journalistic role. As for Trump, his attacks against the mainstream media will continue. Pointless and misguided as his media revenge tour is, it seems to be all he knows how to do. Margaret Sullivan is a Guardian US columnist writing on media, politics and culture

webTitle: The deportation of Milo Yiannopoulos signals a rupture within Maga | Moira Donegan

fields.headline: The deportation of Milo Yiannopoulos signals a rupture within Maga
fields.trailText: The far-right provocateur helped galvanize a movement that no longer needs him. Now his imitators are claiming victory
fields.bodyText: It’s been a long, slow decline for Milo Yiannopoulos. From the vantage point of 2026, it’s easy to forget that he was once a big deal. The British-born far-right provocateur, who was arrested by ICE in Louisiana and deported from the US this week, was among the first media figures to ride the “gamergate” controversy and ensuing rightwing populist wave that brought Donald Trump to office in 2016. An editor of the then ascendant Breitbart News from 2014 to 2017, Yiannopoulous was an early adopter of the media strategy of algorithm-optimized outrage bait, trawling the internet and consulting a large network of well-placed sources in search of stories he could use to fan the flames of online culture war discourses. He would write a story mocking a feminist, or fire off a tweet saying something racist about Muslims, and the ensuing firestorm of controversy would result in online arguments, media coverage, and his own promptly and decisively rising star. Rinse, repeat. Back then, at the start of the Trump era, Yiannopoulous was something of a novelty. Rightwing provocation peddlers had not previously come in his millennial, digitally savvy mold; few others had adopted a fey, gregarious kind of gay male humor for the increasingly theatrical right. But soon, Yiannopoulous was overrun with competitors. The rightwing influencer field became crowded, then saturated. He has spent the past few years at the fringe of the fringe, working for and hobnobbing with a hodgepodge of odious figures who aim to critique Donald Trump from the right, such as the former congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene, the white nationalist streamer Nick Fuentes, and the antisemitic rapper who now goes by Ye. In a particularly pathetic bid for relevance, he once declared himself “ex-gay” and set about promoting conversion therapy. His downfall had been a long time coming. Yiannopoulous, often willing to say in vulgar terms what many parts of the American right were only willing to allude to in polite ones, often found himself overstepping. He was banned from Twitter, then from Facebook; he was banned from Australia. In 2017, he resigned from Breitbart and lost a book deal with Simon and Schuster after comments resurfaced in which he claimed that sexual abuse of children by adults could be consensual and “hugely positive experiences”. Yiannopoulous’s comments, which he later apologized for, are not so far out of line from what some on the far right have said about child marriage, or the need to encourage childbirth among teen girls. But Yiannopoulous was talking about boys, not girls, and by then the Maga movement he had helped to galvanize no longer needed him. There were already plenty of Milo imitators, eager to see a rival deposed and ready to fill his grotesque niche. Several of those imitators are now claiming victory, declaring themselves responsible for Yiannopoulous’s recent deportation. Laura Loomer, a far-right influencer, provocateur and conspiracist in Yiannopoulous’s mold, who has become a confidante of Donald Trump, quickly claimed to have orchestrated Yiannopoulous’s arrest. “I reported him to ICE and the FBI,” Loomer posted. “I told you all that Milo was an illegal alien.” As Anna Merlan of Mother Jones reported, two other far-right influencers – who, unlike Yiannopoulous, are still in good standing with the Maga regime – also claimed to have advance knowledge of the DHS’s plans to remove and deport their enemy: Raheem Kassam, a onetime Breitbart UK editor and current Washington DC restaurateur, and Benny Johnson, a Maga-aligned writer and social media personality. There’s reason to take at least Loomer seriously: last year, Trump fired several high-ranking national security officials after their names appeared on a list of alleged enemies that Loomer presented to him in the Oval Office. If these figures’ boasts are true, this would mean, at best, that at least some figures within the DHS are leaking information about what are supposed to be confidential proceedings to online grifters and grievance peddlers, so that those influencers can get in a bit of satisfying mockery online. At worst, it would mean that the country’s massive federal security apparatus is being deployed to settle internet feuds among crackpot influencers. There’s always a bit of schadenfreude to witnessing these incidents, watching the Trump camp dissolve into infighting and treachery, and seeing the amorality, bigotry or cynical opportunism of those who once sided with Trump be punished with a blow to something those actors actually care about: their own status and careers. By now, there have been so many purges and abrupt reversals of fortune for the once-ascendant members of the Maga coalition that it is hardly worth enumerating them all: Trump, it turns out, has done his purging more frequently and unexpectedly, less a single Night of the Long Knives and more a recurring series of Afternoons of the Mean Tweets. But Yiannoupoulous’s downfall is more than just another case of the Maga revolution eating its children. His abrupt arrest and deportation seems, instead, like the product of a bigger rupture within the Trump movement, wherein the isolationist, anti-Zionist, and increasingly antisemitic faction is in revolt against Trump and the neoconservative, expansionist and pro-Israel and pro-military adventurism wing that persuaded him to go to war with Iran. As the unpopular, unwinnable war drags on, sending prices soaring and making it seem more likely that irate voters will look to punish the Republicans in the November midterms, fingers are pointing within the Maga coalition, as major players look to dilute their own responsibility and find someone else to blame. Milo’s deportation might be just one instance in the much uglier fight to come as these figures seek to throw one another under the bus. If they were honorable people, after all, they wouldn’t be in the Trump camp in the first place. Those of us hoping for a sizable Democratic victory might understandably welcome this outcome. Let them fight; let them tear each other to pieces; let them destroy themselves, and nothing of value will be lost. But there is something gruesome, too, about seeing the government deployed this way. It is humiliating to be ruled over by such people – conspiracists and bigots and idiots, people without virtue or competence or even dignity to match their power. They’re all going to suffer in the ugly infighting that’s coming. But we’re all suffering, too. Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnist

webTitle: ‘If he can make money in a tyranny, that’s fine by him’: Francis Fukuyama on Trump, democracy – and changing his mind

fields.headline: ‘If he can make money in a tyranny, that’s fine by him’: Francis Fukuyama on Trump, democracy – and changing his mind
fields.trailText: The political thinker became famous for declaring the triumph of liberal democracy. Thirty-seven years on, he explains what he really meant and why he made the rare journey from right to left
fields.bodyText: There are not many public intellectuals who can say they’ve been cited by Capt James T Kirk of the Starship Enterprise, but Francis Fukuyama is one of them. In Star Trek VI: The Undiscovered Country, William Shatner’s character is in a reflective mood, and speaks to the Klingon chancellor. “Some people think the future means the end of history,” Kirk muses. “Well, we haven’t run out of history quite yet.” When the film came out in 1991 and in the years that followed, you’d often hear comments like that. They were nods to a thesis so famous it hardly needed spelling out. It debuted in a 15-page essay written by Fukuyama, then a 36-year-old thinktanker, which was published in the National Interest, a right-leaning journal of US foreign policy, in the summer of 1989. There was a question mark in the title: it was called The End of History?. In book form three years later, it became The End of History and the Last Man. But these were subtleties that, as we shall see, got lost. The essay made its author internationally renowned and helped power a career as a political scientist, philosopher and analyst, specialising in foreign policy and political economy. Fukuyama’s counsel was sought by governments and boardrooms worldwide, from the C-suite of Ford to the tent of the Libyan dictator Muammar Gaddafi. But, as is clear from his new memoir – which is less a conventional autobiography than the story of a life in ideas, one that revisits intellectual shifts and academic schisms and which, by contrast, scarcely mentions the author’s 40-year marriage – it also became something of a millstone. I ask how he feels about that article. Perhaps the way the Beatles might have come to regard their breakthrough hit She Loves You: grateful for the success, but tired of having to replay it, again and again. “Well, a little bit of both,” Fukuyama, now 73, says on a video call from California, via a computer which, incidentally, he built himself. “I certainly think that I would not have gotten the attention that I did if I’d used a different title. So that made a difference.” But there has been a downside. “You know, I get these ridiculous comments, on the internet. If I post a picture of my grandkids, they say, ‘Oh, I thought it was the end of grandkids.’” The problem, as Fukuyama sees it, is a 37-year-old misunderstanding – one that took root as soon as the essay was published. Thanks to that simple, memorable phrase – “the end of history” – people assumed that Fukuyama was arguing that, with the cold war winding down and the Berlin Wall about to fall, human conflict, even human events, were drawing to a close. That all the big arguments had been settled, there would be no more war, and the entire world was about to live under US-style liberal democracy. As he puts it in his new book, In the Realm of the Last Man, it was taken to be an expression of “naive liberal triumphalism, and I have been asked several times a week over the past three decades whether I wished to recant my argument. I have written thousands of words and given dozens of interviews seeking to answer this question.” Indeed, he tells me, that was “one of the reasons for writing the memoir: to finally get down in a very clear way what I was intending and the ways I was wrong, and the ways I believe I’m still right.” The book makes clear his argument was a subtle one, drawn from Hegelian thought and inspired by an earlier interpreter of Hegel, Alexandre Kojève, from whom Fukuyama borrowed that all-important title. According to Kojève, the end of history was the moment when a principle or set of ideas emerged that could not be bettered, in terms of their ability to satisfy the human beings who lived in a system shaped by them. Kojève himself had playfully proposed the year 1806 as the end of history, since that was the moment when, thanks to his defeat of the Prussian monarchy in the Battle of Jena-Auerstedt, Napoleon brought the code that bore his name to the heart of old Europe, the legal framework that emerged from the French Revolution. As Fukuyama writes, the revolution of 1789 “established the underlying principles of a modern liberal order, namely, the two principles of liberty and equality, or the equality of liberty”. Of course, those principles were not immediately or fully implemented: even as Napoleon was advancing in central Europe, the French colonial authorities were putting down a slave revolt in Haiti. “But Kojève’s point was that once the idea of universal freedom got out, it was only a matter of time before those principles became accepted and practised around the world.” Even if the time it took was measured in centuries, with plenty of events – including two world wars – along the way. This was the nature of the argument Fukuyama was making for 1989. Not that liberal democracy was perfect or that it had been achieved everywhere and that all conflict was over. But rather that the evidence had become compelling that there was no better guiding principle or system. And Fukuyama still maintains that view. “For the last 30-odd years, I’ve been saying that I’m looking for an alternative system that purports to be more humanly satisfying than liberal democracy. And a number of candidates have come along. Some of them, I think, are very implausible.” He cites Iranian-style theocracy as one such candidate. The Chinese model is a more serious contender. As an authoritarian system, he says, it can make decisions more efficiently than liberal democracy. “So the question for me is: is this also a sustainable system? Are we going to see this [replicated] in other places in 30 years? And that is still an open question.” If, over the next generation or so, China turns out to be much more successful than the US, with an exportable model that satisfies human needs, then Fukuyama promises he will be “perfectly happy to concede that I was wrong on the fundamental premise”. He also accepts that the current consensus on liberal democracy is far from universal, and that the “liberal” part of that idea – the belief in constraints and checks on elected power – is especially vulnerable. He writes that is in part because support for those constraints has often been contingent on a collective memory of how dangerous the world can become without them. A younger generation who have known only peace and prosperity, and for whom the tyrannies of the mid-20th century are ancient history, will only be dimly aware of the perils of unrestrained, illiberal rule. But surely Donald Trump, born just one year after the defeat of nazism, is living proof that proximity to that dark history hardly entails respect for the guardrails imposed by liberal democracy? How do we explain the US president’s disregard for that danger? “You know, that is one of the great psychological questions that future historians are going to have to answer. He has had this weird attraction not just to the current Russia and Vladimir Putin but, all the way back in the 1980s, he visited Moscow. He took out these full-page ads attacking Nato way back then, when we were still in the middle of the cold war. I mean, it somehow has to do with his lack of any kind of moral compass beyond his own self-interest. He basically worries about whether he can make money, and if you can make money in a tyranny, that’s fine with him.” It’s worth getting to the bottom of what Fukuyama meant all those years ago because, once you’re there, you find an idea more interesting than the soundbite versions of his thesis ever allowed. The final paragraph of his original essay declared: “The end of history will be a very sad time.” With the fundamental question of politics essentially resolved, even if far from realised, “the worldwide ideological struggle that called forth daring, courage, imagination and idealism, will be replaced by economic calculation, the endless solving of technical problems, environmental concerns, and the satisfaction of sophisticated consumer demands.” As Fukuyama writes now: “The being who emerges at the end of history is typically someone stripped of struggle, risk and ambition, someone whom the philosopher Nietzsche labeled the ‘Last Man’. We have been living in the realm of the Last Man for some time now.” Once this notion is unpacked, even those who dispute Fukuyama’s reading of 1989 will concede that he had an uncanny inkling of what was to come. For what he was anticipating was that liberal democratic societies might prove adept at delivering stability and relative material comfort, but that would still leave something profound missing. He cites Socrates’ notion of thymos, or spiritedness: that part of the soul which desires the respect or esteem of other human beings. The last man might have his basic economic needs met, but he would become angry if he believed he was not receiving the recognition that was his due. It amounts to the simple craving for one’s equal dignity to be respected. Reading those passages, it’s hard not to think of the worldwide surge of nationalist populism and the Maga movement in particular. “The mass of the people that come to Donald Trump’s rallies feel that the liberal elites have not been respecting them,” says Fukuyama. “One of the things that propelled Trump to the top of the American political system is his recognition that they were being disrespected, and he found a way of talking to them in a manner that didn’t show that kind of contempt. He doesn’t use big words. He tells stupid stories that they think are very funny, and you know, educated people are appalled by.” This, he says, is a key challenge for Democrats. “If you really want to solve this problem of equally distributed respect … it’s about both listening and talking. I think a lot of elite politicians actually don’t listen to people that are not like themselves. They don’t necessarily listen to ordinary people, and they also don’t know how to speak to ordinary people.” He notes the desperation of Democrats “looking for working-class candidates that they can push” in the November midterm elections, but says the “equal distribution of respect requires both policies that distribute actual material benefits more equally and a different kind of political discourse”. In that context, he likes the look of former Chicago mayor and potential 2028 presidential candidate Rahm Emanuel, a man with a streetfighter’s manner who is also, says Fukuyama, “very funny”. The other defining trait of the last man is the hunger for a cause, for a life-or-death struggle that might give his life meaning. In 1989, Fukuyama anticipated “a powerful nostalgia” for the age when such battles raged, and that too reads like a premonition of our own era. “Fundamentally we’re living in a really weird time,” he says now. He looks back to Germany of the 1930s. “They’d just lost a horrendous war, millions of casualties. Then hyperinflation. Everybody’s savings get wiped out. You have instability on the streets of the Weimar Republic, and so – it’s not an excuse – but you can kind of understand why people would be drawn to extremist ideologies at that point. But that’s not the world we’re living in in 2026. You know, we’re actually pretty stable, peaceful. And yet you find people on both the left and the right that are saying, ‘This is the worst possible world.’ In America we have the Maga right that says that America is dying. It’s being killed by the other side. And it’s very hard to understand how they can argue that with any kind of historical awareness.” For the left, at least, hasn’t the climate crisis played a part in contributing to that mood of existential doom? Fukuyama doubts it. “I am sitting in California. It’s a comfortable 70 degrees [21C]. You know, I’m not burning up like you in Europe, so maybe it’s just my personal situation. But I think that climate still remains a rather abstract thing for many people.” He points the finger in a different direction. “Social media and the internet in general have permitted this vast disconnect between actual material lived reality and what people experience online.” He cites the legions of young men in the manosphere, gaming the days away, simultaneously fed a falsely bleak picture of the world and longing for a cause worth dying for, as an illustration of the phenomenon he warned of in the very last sentence of the 1989 essay: “Perhaps this very prospect of centuries of boredom at the end of history will serve to get history started once again.” There’s a chapter in the new book whose title hints at the other story the memoir tells: On Changing Your Mind. Fukuyama has made the relatively rare political journey from right to left. A former official in the Reagan and Bush administrations, he tells of his time as a disciple of the noted conservative scholar Allan Bloom and as part of the neoconservative gang of thinkers who prepared the intellectual ground for the 2003 invasion of Iraq. Fukuyama renounced his support for that war in February 2004. In the book, he candidly admits that what prevented him from making the break earlier was, in part, less ideological than social and human: he didn’t want to end friendships he had cherished. Still, his departure from the right was not solely in the sphere of foreign policy. While his former colleagues could only see government as an obstacle to be cleared out of the way, his own studies of societies around the world led him to regard a capable state as essential. As if to confirm how far he has travelled, one chapter of the book is titled Learning to Love Bureaucrats. I ask whether his perspective on the world might have differed from other Republicans and conservatives because of his Japanese-American roots, which are detailed affectingly in the book. It tells of his grandmother, a “picture bride” who left Japan at 21 when she was put on a “steamer to Los Angeles all alone, where she was to marry a stranger 10 years older than herself”, and of an uncle left “penniless” after the store he built was effectively confiscated when he, like all Japanese-Americans on the west coast, was interned during the second world war. Did he see things differently because he was a member of an ethnic minority that had suffered a bitter history of exclusion? “No, I don’t think so,” he says immediately. “I’ve tried to avoid thinking of myself as an Asian-American my whole life, because I just don’t like that sort of identity politics. It’s true that, after 11 September, you had certain rightwing people in the United States saying, ‘Well, we ought to put Arab-Americans in camps.’ And, yeah, of course, I felt that that was really wrong based on my family history, but I don’t think that made me especially sensitive to those sorts of issues.” What changed his mind was a changing world. Even if he still thinks the big question has been resolved, events matter. The Iraq war and the crash of 2008 upended his worldview. As he puts it, “If you’re an intellectual and you believe certain things about the use of military force in foreign policy and about unregulated markets in economics, and both of them lead to big disasters, you ought to rethink some of those assumptions.” For Francis Fukuyama, an end to history never meant an end to thinking. • In the Realm of the Last Man by Francis Fukuyama is published by Profile Books (£20) and is out on 8 September. To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply. • Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? webTitle: ‘Dangerous power grab’: top Democrats decry USPS system that could thwart mail-in voting – as it happened

fields.headline: ‘Dangerous power grab’: top Democrats decry USPS system that could thwart mail-in voting – as it happened
fields.trailText: This live blog is now closed.
fields.bodyText: We’re wrapping up our live coverage for the day. Here are today’s key developments in US politics: Senator Ed Markey won the Democratic primary in Massachusetts, beating back a challenge from Seth Moulton, who argued his opponent was too old to be effective at his job. Progressive lawmakers and the organization Our Revolution hailed the victory. Democratic leaders in the US House sharply criticized two representatives for defecting and joining with Republicans in order to advance a procedural vote, describing it as a “significant breach of trust,” that requires “a serious response”. The US House of Representative voted to censure Chuck Edwards, a Republican congressman who the ethics committee found violated rules against sexual harassment in his conduct towards two young female staffers. The Trump administration seized on House Democrats voting against a resolution denouncing socialism, condemning the lawmakers as “sick [and] dangerous”. The resolution included language calling for the enactment of Trump’s SAVE America Act, a strict voting bill that would ban mail-in ballots and require voters to prove their citizenship. Donald Trump announced that he will nominate Hung Cao to serve as the next secretary of the US Navy. Kathy Hochul, New York’s governor, criticized Donald Trump for withholding $87m in counterterrorism funds from the state, describing the move as a betrayal of 9/11 victims. Donald Trump’s Department of Homeland Security has apparently taken steps to advance the president’s efforts to limit voting. The US Department of Justice announced that its antitrust division was expanding its investigation of beef prices to include eight of the country’s largest grocers. The associate attorney general Stanley Woodward sent letters about recent rising costs to companies including Amazon, Walmart, Costco, Kroger, Publix, Albertsons, Aldi and Ahold Delhaize USA, the DoJ said. Donald Trump has also accused meatpacking companies ⁠of driving up costs. Our Revolution, the political group founded by Bernie Sanders after his 2016 campaign, hailed Ed Markey’s victory in the Massachusetts Democratic Senate primary. “Tonight’s victory isn’t just a win for Ed Markey or for our progressive movement. It’s a rejection of the idea that generational change has to come at the expense of bold, progressive leadership,” Joseph Geevarghese, the organization’s executive director, said in a statement. “From staking his political capital on the Green New Deal, to fighting for Medicare for All, abolishing ICE and taking on the corporations and billionaires rigging our economy, Ed has consistently been willing to go where the Democratic Party needs to go — often before the rest of Washington gets there.” Democratic leaders in the US House sharply criticized two representatives for defecting and joining with Republicans in order to advance a procedural vote. “The decision by two of our colleagues to blindside the entire House Democratic Caucus and join with the Republican majority to pass a procedural rule on the brink of failing represents a significant breach of trust,” Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, whip Katherine Clark and Pete Aguilar, the caucus chair, said in a statement. “It is an action that necessitates a serious response, and we have asked the Committee on Caucus Rules to take this up in short order.” The statement was referring to moderates Marie Gluesenkamp Perez and Jared Golden. The bills included a resolution condemning socialism, which also called for the enactment of Trump’s SAVE America Act, that eight Democrats voted to pass. Hakeem Jeffries condemned the Trump administration in response to the death of Pierre Damas Bel, a Haitian college student who died by suicide after he lost his legal status and was required to wear an ankle monitor. “Like hundreds of thousands of Haitians, Pierre fled dangerous conditions and received temporary protected status to build a better life for himself and patriotically contribute to our nation,” the House Democratic leader said, describing the administration’s actions as “despiable cruelty”. “Instead, Donald Trump’s mass deportation machine ripped away Pierre’s legal status, threatened him with terrifying violence, forced him to wear an ankle monitor and humiliated him in front of his peers.” Bel, a 20-year-old who came to the US in 2024 and lost his temporary protected status in July, died on Monday. NBC News reported that while Bel’s immigration case made its way through the courts ICE required he wear an ankle monitor. Bel said he was “humiliated” by the experience and was bullied. Senator Ed Markey won the Democratic primary in Massachusetts on Tuesday, beating back a challenge from Seth Moulton, a congressman who tried to unseat him by arguing to voters his opponent was too old to be effective at his job. Massachusetts is heavily Democratic, making the senator favored to win a third full term in the November general election, where he faces the Republican nominee John Deaton. The 80-year-old incumbent, according to the Associated Press, easily defeated his 47-year-old rival, at a moment when Democratic voters agonize over the age of some lawmakers, a concern that was amplified by Joe Biden’s disastrous re-election bid in 2024, and Kamala Harris’s subsequent failure to keep Donald Trump from returning to the White House. The Trump administration seized on House Democrats voting against a resolution denouncing socialism, condemning the lawmakers as “sick [and] dangerous”. But there was more in the resolution than language critical of socialism “in all its forms”. The Associated Press reports that it called for the enactment of Trump’s SAVE America Act, a strict voting bill that would ban mail-in ballots and require voters to prove their citizenship. The measure was approved approved 220-192 with a handful of Democrats joining with Republicans in support of the resolution. Democrats described the resolution as a trap ahead of the US midterm elections. “This isn’t a serious bill,” Congressman Josh Gottheimer told Axios. The New Jersey representative is a moderate who has criticized Democratic Socialism. “If you actually want to take on socialism instead of playing political games, you don’t slip in the SAVE [America] Act as a poison pill that you know no Democrat will vote for.” Polls have just closed in Massachusetts where progressive Ed Markey, 80, faces a younger challenger in the US Senate Democratic primary in what is being described as a generational fight. His rival US representative Seth Moulton has argued Markey is too old to serve another term. Read more on the race here: Donald Trump announced on Tuesday that he will nominate Hung Cao to serve as the next secretary of the US Navy. Cao, a former Senate candidate in Virginia and retired navy captain, has been the acting secretary since April and was previously the under secretary. “The Senate needs to confirm this Warfighter, ASAP, so he can continue the fantastic work he has been doing over the past 4 months,” Trump said of the nomination. The news comes amid a shake up in US military leadership under defense secretary Pete Hegseth. This week army secretary Daniel Driscoll left his role after 18 months on the job, prompting Democrats to accuse Hegseth of having “hollowed out” the army’s senior ranks. The US House of Representative has voted to censure Chuck Edwards, a Republican congressman who the ethics committee found violated rules against sexual harassment in his conduct towards two young female staffers. The vote was 413-2, with 207 Republicans joining 205 Democrats. The largely ceremonial punishment saw Edwards stand in the well of the House chamber and be read the resolution. First elected in 2022 to represent a western North Carolina district, Edwards dropped his bid for re-election following the release of the bipartisan panel’s determination that he “may have created or fostered a hostile work environment and engaged in sexual harassment” by giving gifts and lavishing attention on the two women. “A member of Congress should not single out a staffer and isolate them from other staff, make frequent comments regarding that person’s appearance and weight, send messages in the middle of the night, text staff deeply personal and seemingly romantic thoughts, intrude on personal occasions without invitation, pay for personal vacations, and spend thousands of dollars on gifts for staffers,” the report read. In a speech on the House floor before the vote, Edwards defended himself, noting that the committee found he did not engage in sexual activity with the staffers or suggested it. He argued the ethics committee overreached in its conclusions, while apologizing both to the unnamed staffers and his wife. “Regret is not an admission of sexual harassment, I can acknowledge poor judgment, regret the discomfort that some of my actions may have caused, and apologize to those who were hurt by this episode, while still disputing a conclusion that the evidence just simply does not support,” Edwards said. North Carolina Republicans have replaced him on the ballot with state representative Jennifer Balkcom, who will face the Democratic nominee Jamie Ager in the November midterms. Kathy Hochul, New York’s governor, criticized Donald Trump for withholding $87m in counterterrorism funds from the state, describing the move as a betrayal of 9/11 victims. “Don’t undermine our public safety efforts. Don’t defund the police who thwart terror attacks. Don’t play political games with people’s lives,” Hochul said at a press conference on Tuesday alongside Mayor Zohran Mamdani. The funding is essential to keeping New Yorkers safe, Mamdani said, adding that it funds 12 bomb squads across the city, among other programs. The US Department of Homeland Security told CBS News Hochul “is manufacturing a funding crisis” and accused Hochul and Mamdani of “[shielding] criminals from the law”. “New York works with federal law enforcement every day to take dangerous criminals off the streets. So spare us the theatrics,” Hochul said in response. “And while you’re here, cut the $87 million check you owe our cops and counterterrorism officials.” The MapQuest app jumped to No 1 on US Apple after defying Donald Trump’s move to rename Lake Ontario as trade tensions between the US and Canada continue to escalate. The 30-year-old company has found itself in the spotlight for dismissing the president’s executive order that directed federal agencies to use “Lake America” to refer to the smallest of the Great Lakes. Read more here: Donald Trump will meet with oil refiners and distributors as part of what the president described as an effort to increase US refining capacity and lower gas prices. Since the war with Iran began earlier this year, gas prices in the US have risen more than 30%, hitting American consumers hard. Trump has at various points argued that gas prices were not particularly high, increased costs at the pump were a small price to pay to stop Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon and that oil companies have made too much money from the conflict. In a statement posted on social media, the president said he was “laser-focused” on ensuring his “energy dominance” agenda brings the “most cost savings possible at the pump”. Donald Trump’s Department of Homeland Security has apparently taken steps to advance the president’s efforts to limit voting. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) now has a webpage with a blue box that reads “Coming Soon” and “State Citizen Lists Portal.” According to Democracy Docket, this webpage is newly published. This portal is in keeping with Trump’s March executive order mandating that DHS and the Social Security Administration gather data and compose lists of eligible voters from all 50 states. Democracy Docket notes that a DHS memo released in June said the department plans on having this portal up and running by 4 September. Voting rights advocates have insisted that federal authorities lack the legal power to make and manage lists of voters. A federal voter eligibility database has not existed previously as US states and localities are supposed to manage elections, Democracy Docket explained. Donald Trump’s airplane catering truck caper is getting the Netflix treatment. The streaming service announced Tuesday on X that “Instadocs: The Decoy Plane,” would premier on 4 September. The program “unpacks the incident through firsthand accounts from members of the press corps who were aboard Air Force One as well as a former Secret Service agent and a former Air Force One crew member.” Trump was secretly transported to a different plane from the one press and public believed he would take to depart Turkey in July. The decision to switch planes came after US intelligence purportedly found a credible threat that Iran wanted to kill him. Trump exited Air Force One in a catering truck, a move first reported by the Washington Post and New York Times. More than one hundred reporters, officials, and aides were kept on this plane. They were not apprised that there was a threat to their lives. Two congressional Democrats are demanding that a government watchdog probe the Trump administration’s use of an obscure law to surreptitiously gather records on journalists, unions, and non-profits – without judicial oversight. The Guardian’s Sam Levine exclusively reports that Oregon Senator Ron Wyden and Rep Pramila Jayapal of Washington sent their request to the government accountability office (GAO), the non-partisan congressional watchdog. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) recently employed its ability to issue administrative summonses for customs matters to demand information. They wrote in their request: “Crucially, the recipients of these subpoenas – often third-party companies and service providers – maintain a first amendment right to notify their customers of the demand, allowing the actual targets of the subpoenas the opportunity to assert their own legal rights or challenge the demand in court … We request an audit of HSI’s use of non-disclosure language in immigration subpoenas and customs summonses, as well as the circumstances under which HSI has used customs summonses unrelated to import violations or customs duties. President Trump seems to think there’s no point in reaching a deal with Iran. “I think ‌an agreement with them isn’t worth the paper it’s written on. ⁠We gave them a lot of chances,” Trump told Fox News. His comments come as US strikes on Iran resumed Tuesday amid allegations that the country was trying to put mines in the strait of Hormuz. Trump said that the strikes would intensify greatly if Iran retaliated. The US House on Tuesday passed a short-term funding bill that will keep the federal government operating at current levels until 11 December. This bill, which has already been green-lighted by the US Senate, will now go to President Trump’s desk. If Trump signs the legislation, this will postpone more permanent funding discussions until after the midterm elections, per NBC News. Democrats and Republicans have quarreled over the extent of federal spending in their talks to forge a one-year deal. Democrats, for example, rebuffed Trump’s demands for a $1.5bn military budget – up significantly from the record $1 bn military budget approved in 2025. After the US announced Tuesday that it is striking targets in Iran, President Trump threatened “much harder” action if the country retaliated. “They will be hit again at a much harder and higher level, but it will not be the biggest attack of them all, that is waiting in the wings and, when it is over, there will be very little left of the Islamic Republic of Iran,” Trump said on Truth Social. Trump said on his social media platform that the US strikes were in response to Iran’s alleged failed effort to place mines in the strait of Hormuz. He also said the strikes were responsive to Iran’s intercepted attack on a US base in Jordan. Trump’s comments bring to mind his past statements about attacks on Iran that could constitute war crimes if conducted, such as threatening numerous times to destroy critical civilian infrastructure and to bomb Iran “back to the Stone Ages.” Trump also made a now notorious threat in April that “a whole civilization will die tonight” if they didn’t reach a deal. Donald Trump has appointed a Christian pastor to advise his administration on tobacco health concerns. “I am pleased to announce that Pastor Darrell Scott, a longtime friend, respected Faith Leader, and tireless Advocate for America’s Underserved Communities, will be serving my Administration and me as an Advisor for tobacco health issues on the Advisory Committee to the Director (ACD) in the CDC,” Trump said in a Tuesday afternoon Truth Social post. Trump said that “for far too long, tobacco-related disease has taken an enormous toll on American Families, including Communities that have too often been overlooked and underserved.” Scott, Trump said, “understands these Communities, and the challenges they face, and he knows how to bring people together to get RESULTS.” Trump said that in keeping with a campaign promise, Scott’s appointment will support “solutions to reduce harm and SAVE LIVES.” The president wrapped his post by saying “MAKE AMERICA HEALTHY AND SAFE AGAIN!” Scott has long had a reputation as being one of Trump’s earliest and dedicated Black supporters. Trump in 2016 thanked Scott for encouraging his presidential run. In 2018, Scott called Trump “the most pro-Black president we’ve had in our lifetime”. Scott co-founded the National Diversity Coalition with Michael Cohen, who was the prosecution’s star witness at Trump’s New York hush-money trial. The coalition marked a clunky effort during the 2016 race to show that he had support from Black and Latinx voters. The US oil behemoth Chevron is poised to increase operations in Venezuela, The Associated Press reported on Tuesday. The AP, citing a US official who told reporters about Chevron’s planned announcement, said the petroleum giant’s officials and US energy secretary Chris Wright are meant to travel to Venezuela on Wednesday. There, Chevron’s new investment is expected to officially be revealed. Chevron, which according to the AP is the second-largest US oil concern, presently has one “major presence” in Venezuela. The White House on Monday confirmed that it is teaming up with North American Blue Energy Partners in keeping with Donald Trump’s efforts to capitalize on Venezuela’s oil industry. Another Democrat senator is sounding the alarm following a whistleblower report on the US Postal Service’s hasty efforts to comply with Trump’s order on mail-in voting. Arizona’s Ruben Gallego, also said he wanted postal officials to answer questions under oath. “A whistleblower just confirmed Trump’s mail-ballot verification system is broken enough to lose or reject people’s ballots ahead of the midterms,” Gallego said in a statement. “I am calling for an immediate stop to this rollout, and I am demanding that USPS leadership come before Congress to testify under oath.” “The American people deserve answers before a single ballot is put at risk.” The US military has said it is striking targets in Iran over attempted attacks on shipping as hostilities flare after a month. US Central Command said in an update on X: Today at 12 p.m. ET, U.S. forces began striking Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targets in Iran. The strikes follow recent attempted attacks by the IRGC against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members deployed to the region. Canadian PM Mark Carney has rebuked Donald Trump’s administration and urged officials in Washington to “start being serious” amid escalating trade tensions between the US and Canada. Days before Canada is due to retaliate against Trump’s sweeping tariffs with its own duties on US goods, Carney criticized US officials for insulting his country. “It is beneath their office,” he said. “When the Americans stop doing memes, stop throwing shade, stop trying to be tough and start being serious about having those discussions, we can have those discussions” about trade, Carney said. Here’s our report. US trade representative Jamieson Greer also today downplayed the potentially disastrous impact of a trade war with Canada, telling Politico: “It’s more their emergency than ours.” He added: “There are no negotiations happening on trade right now.” More from the interview here and here. Democrats have decried Trump’s “dangerous power grab” following the disclosure of a whistleblower report alleging the US Postal Service is poised to launch a computer system that could derail mail-in voting. Representative Robert Garcia, ranking member of the committee on oversight and government reform, said in a statement: “This new secret tracking system at the US Postal Service is faulty, untested, and threatens to totally disrupt ballot delivery for millions of American citizens. We are fighting in court to protect the right to vote by mail for all and will continue to investigate. This unconstitutional and dangerous power grab must be permanently and immediately blocked.” More reactions here and here. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) is planning to ramp up voter fraud investigations in several states beginning today, according to CNN. DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin has intensified efforts to make his department integral to voter fraud investigations per CNN, which cited “internal federal guidance” in its reporting. The department has allegedly “leaned on” one of its agencies, Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), to pursue this work. More here. As we’ve been reporting, Democrats have been speaking out following the disclosure of a whistleblower report alleging the US Postal Service is poised to launch a computer system that could derail mail-in voting. Virginia senator Mark Warner wrote on X: Wow. A whistleblower is confirming our fears: millions of Americans may not receive their mail-in ballot ahead of the midterm elections thanks to Trump’s new policies. They are openly trying to silence your vote. We will keep fighting back. And according to an NBC News reporter on X, California representative Ted Lieu told a press conference this morning: “Just go fucking vote. The Trump administration is going to try to suppress your vote.” Donald Trump’s Department of Homeland Security (DHS) is planning to ramp up voter fraud investigations in several states beginning Tuesday, according to CNN. DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin has intensified efforts to make his department integral to voter fraud investigations per CNN, which cited “internal federal guidance” in its reporting. The department has allegedly “leaned on” one of its agencies, Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), to pursue this work. HSI, which traditionally has pursued major crimes such as human trafficking or drug smuggling, now has an “unprecedented number of agents” to work on voter fraud probes. This includes tracking down voting records for people who are believed to be non-citizens, CNN said. Asked for comment, a DHS spokesperson said: “While ICE Homeland Security Investigations is not able to comment on any active investigations, HSI is actively rooting out and investigating election fraud wherever it can be found. We have repeatedly demonstrated that illegal aliens can and do vote in our elections. Under President Trump, HSI is committed to restoring integrity to our election systems and ensuring that American citizens and only American citizens are electing American leaders.” While Trump has repeatedly sounded the alarm about voter fraud, experts say that instances of voter fraud are exceedingly rare. Trump has nonetheless used false claims about widespread election fraud to bolster his crackdown on voting access. He signed an executive order this spring that limits mail-in voting. That order requires that the US Postal Service to come up with a national voter file. Under this order, the USPS also has to come up with a process requiring states to tell them which voters want a mail-in ballot – and bar them from receiving one if they’re not on the postal agency’s approved voter list. Democratic senator Jack Reed voiced grave concern about US Army secretary Dan Driscoll’s resignation amid ongoing Defense Department turmoil. “I do not welcome Secretary Driscoll’s resignation. His departure leaves the Army without its top civilian and uniformed leaders, and a military service whose leadership ranks have been gutted by Secretary Hegseth,” the Rhode Island senator said in a statement, after thanking Driscoll for his service, including work to strengthen the army. “I am alarmed that Secretary Driscoll’s leadership of the Army stands in stark contrast to Secretary Hegseth’s disastrous tenure atop the Defense Department.” “It is far past time for President Trump to recognize the lasting harm that Pete Hegseth is inflicting on the Department of Defense,” he also said. “At this moment, hundreds of thousands of soldiers are deployed around the world, many in combat zones. The soldiers carrying out these missions deserve leadership that is reliable, forthright, and focused on the fight ahead,” the statement continued. “The Army cannot stay ahead of our adversaries while its senior ranks are hollowed out and its chain of command is left in limbo.” Hegseth has faced continued criticism for his handling of US military activity, such as the war in Iran. The Washington Post reported that senior US military commanders routinely voice formal objections – but that Hegseth goes forward with his ideas despite these objections. The Post reported, for example, that top military officials opposed prolonging the war in Iran. The Pentagon has rejected this reporting. Representative Robert Garcia, ranking member of the committee on oversight and government reform, is speaking out following disclosure of a whistleblower report alleging the US Postal Service is poised to launch a computer system that could derail mail-in voting. Democratic senator Richard Blumenthal disclosed this whistleblower statement, which warned of potential mail-in voting chaos, on Tuesday. “The Oversight Committee has received whistleblower reports that President Trump’s attack on vote-by-mail for the 2026 election is more serious than previously understood,” Garcia said in a statement. “This new secret tracking system at the US Postal Service is faulty, untested, and threatens to totally disrupt ballot delivery for millions of American citizens.” “We are fighting in court to protect the right to vote by mail for all and will continue to investigate. This unconstitutional and dangerous power grab must be permanently and immediately blocked.” Donald Trump in March signed an executive order requiring the creation of a national voter file. Trump’s executive order mandated that the US Postal Service make rules about a process that would require states to apprise them of voters who want mail-in ballots. Trump’s executive order would require that the Postal Service prevent these voters from receiving mail-in ballots unless they are on a the USPS-approved eligible voter list. While the US Supreme Court paved the way for Trump’s efforts to limit mail-in voting, the issue is still being litigated in lower courts. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer also slammed what he claimed were Trump-backed efforts to derail the mail-in voting. “A whistleblower is warning of a ‘catastrophic failure’ in our mail-ballot system—all because Trump is turning USPS into a voter suppression machine,” the New York Democrat said on X. “Vote-by-mail is safe and secure. Trump himself voted by mail just last month.
